alt: Sensation is the detection of physical energy by the sense organs, such as light reaching the retina, and is the same for anyone with working senses. Perception is the brain's organisation and interpretation of that input, and can differ between people looking at the same thing.
caption: Sensation detects; perception interprets, which is why two people can see the same thing differently.

alt: A view from a train window. Near fence posts flash past quickly, shown by a thick arrow, while distant hills drift slowly, shown by a thin arrow. Gibson argued the difference in speed tells us directly how far away things are. Cards summarise his bottom-up theory, a strength and a limitation.
caption: Near objects race past and far ones drift: speed difference is direct information about distance.

alt: Six simplified illusions with their explanations: the Müller-Lyer and Ponzo illusions are misinterpreted depth cues; the Ames Room is size constancy misapplied; Rubin's vase and the Necker cube are ambiguity; the Kanizsa triangle is fiction, because the brain adds edges that are not drawn.
caption: Each illusion is explained by one of four terms: ambiguity, misinterpreted depth cues, fiction or size constancy.

alt: A Ponzo figure: two equal bars between converging lines, the upper one looking longer. Four steps: the converging lines are read as linear perspective, past experience says the upper bar is further away, and a further object with the same retinal image must be bigger. For the Müller-Lyer illusion, fins out resemble the inside corner of a room and fins in the outside corner of a building.
caption: For Gregory, illusions show the brain inferring from cues and experience, and sometimes getting it wrong.

alt: A comparison table. Gibson's bottom-up theory says input contains enough information, picked up directly, supported by motion parallax but weak on illusions. Gregory's top-down theory says input is incomplete and the brain infers from cues and past experience, supported by illusions and perceptual set but based on artificial images. A note suggests the theories can be combined.
caption: Gibson: bottom-up and direct. Gregory: top-down and inferred. Each fits different conditions.

after: ## Perceptual set and the four named studies
alt: Bruner and Minturn: the same ambiguous figure was seen as B among the letters A and C, and as 13 among the numbers 12 and 14. Cards summarise motivation (hungry participants rated food pictures brighter), emotion (briefly flashed shapes were later preferred), culture (holistic versus analytic perception) and an evaluation of the studies.
caption: Expectation, motivation, emotion and culture each create a readiness to see things a certain way.
